section.title: Graphs and transformations
section.p: A function is an assignment. A graph is a picture of all those assignments at once.
Each point on the graph of y=f(x) has the form
The horizontal coordinate is the input. The vertical coordinate is the output.
A graph can show things a formula hides: where a function is positive, where it is zero, where it grows large, and where it has symmetry. It also helps us build new functions from old ones.

exercise.title: Why does changing the input shift the graph the wrong way?

statement.p: Adding outside a function, as in f(x)+3, moves the graph up. Changing the input, as in f(x-2), moves the graph right. In your own words, why do inside changes feel backward, and what question should you ask of the expression inside the function?

hint.p: An outside change alters outputs after the old function has spoken. An inside change asks what new input must be fed to the old function in order to recover an old output.

So an odd function whose graph includes x=0 must pass through the origin.

Symmetry is not only pretty. It saves work. If an even function is known for x\ge 0, then it is known for x\le 0. If an odd function is known for x\ge 0, then the other half is determined by sign change.

exercise.title: What does even or odd symmetry remember?

statement.p: An even function satisfies f(-x)=f(x); an odd function satisfies f(-x)=-f(x). In your own words, what geometric memory does each condition encode, and why does knowing one half of such a graph determine the other half?

hint.p: Evenness is mirror symmetry across the vertical axis. Oddness is a 180^\circ rotation about the origin. Each rule tells you how the output at -x is determined by the output at x.

subsection.title: Reading intercepts, sign, and intervals from a graph
subsection.p: A graph is a picture of outputs. But many questions about a function are really questions about intervals of inputs.
The graph answers these questions visually.

note.title: Reading a graph
note.p: The domain is the set of x-values covered by the graph.
The range is the set of y-values reached by the graph.
The x-intercepts are the points where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis. They occur when
The function is positive where the graph lies above the x-axis, and negative where it lies below the x-axis.

exercise.title: What questions can a graph answer about intervals of inputs?

statement.p: A graph is a picture of outputs, but many questions about a function are really questions about intervals of inputs. In your own words, how do you read domain, range, intercepts, and sign from a graph?

hint.p: Domain is the horizontal coverage. Range is the vertical coverage. Zeros are where the graph meets the input axis. Sign is whether the graph sits above or below that axis.

Calculus will often turn a question about a whole graph into questions about intervals. Where is the function increasing? Where is it decreasing? Where is it concave up? Where does it have a largest value?
For now, we only need the first graph-reading skills: intercepts, sign, domain, range, and transformations.

subsection.title: A graph can suggest, but not prove
subsection.p: Graphs are honest when drawn carefully, but they are not proofs by themselves.
A graphing window can hide behavior. A curve may cross the axis just outside the window. A tiny wiggle may disappear if the scale is too large. A vertical asymptote may look like a steep line.
For example, the functions
and
can look almost identical in a wide viewing window. But the second function has many small oscillations.
The lesson is not to distrust graphs. The lesson is to use them correctly.

definition.title: Graphs guide the eye. Algebra and definitions check the claim

subsection.p: Transformations let us build many new functions from one familiar function. Next we will build functions in a more algebraic way: by adding, multiplying, dividing, and composing them. Composition is the most hidden of these operations, and later it will force one of the most important derivative rules in calculus.

exercise.title: Why can a graph suggest a claim without proving it?

statement.p: A viewing window can hide a crossing, swallow a tiny wiggle, or make an asymptote look like a steep line. In your own words, what is a graph good for, and what must algebra or a definition still check?

hint.p: Graphs guide the eye. They are honest only at the scale and window you chose. A proof has to survive every allowed input, not only the ones that happened to be drawn.
